Question: Each of the sides of a square \(S_1\) with area \(16\) is bisected, and a smaller square \(S_2\) is constructed using the bisection points as vertices. The same process is carried out on \(S_2\) to construct an even smaller square \(S_3.\) What is the area of \(S_3?\)
Solution:
Joining a square's side midpoints leaves four right triangles outside the new square, one at each corner. Calculating their areas shows how much area each construction removes.

Let the parent square have side length \(s>0\). Each corner triangle has perpendicular legs \(s/2\), so its area is
\[
\frac12\cdot\frac{s}{2}\cdot\frac{s}{2}
=\frac{s^2}{8}.
\]
The four triangles have disjoint interiors and, together with the new square, fill the parent square. Their total area is \(4(s^2/8)=s^2/2\). The new square therefore has area
\[
s^2-\frac{s^2}{2}=\frac{s^2}{2},
\]
exactly half the parent's area.

There are two constructions from \(S_1\) to \(S_3\), so the required area is
\[
16\cdot\frac12\cdot\frac12=\boxed{4},
\]
choice \(\boxed{\text{E}}\).
